topic: Stalls, spins and loss of control (SS30)
summary: A stall depends on angle of attack, not speed or attitude, so it can happen at any speed or attitude. Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor: a 60° banked level turn is 2 g, so a 50 kt stall speed becomes about 70 kt. Recovery is: lower the nose, level the wings, full power, accelerate, balance with rudder. A spin needs much more height to recover. Built from CAA Safety Sense Leaflet 30.
src: Safety Sense Leaflet 30: Loss of Control
sections: What a stall is
A stall is controlled by the wing's angle of attack (AoA), not by airspeed alone
It can happen at any attitude or airspeed, including with high control forces
A spin can follow if there is significant yaw during a stall. Recovery needs far more height than a stall
Warning of an approaching stall may be reduced in turns or at higher g
Load factor and stall speed
Stall speed rises with the square root of load factor
60° bank in a level turn = 2 g, so stall speed rises by sqrt 2 (about 1.4)
Example: 50 kt becomes about 70 kt
Common causes
Distraction and fixation: traffic, warnings, late turn to final with too much bank, unexpected ATC instructions
Engine failure on take-off: speed decays quickly, so lower the nose at once. Turning back or stretching the glide often causes a stall
Go-around: abrupt pitch and power changes, so watch airspeed even at full power
VFR into IMC: spatial disorientation leads to loss of control
Symptoms
Approaching stall: rising nose attitude, falling airspeed, buffet, possible warning
Developed stall: low airspeed, nose drop, strong buffet, roll or yaw, sloppy controls, high rate of descent even with a high nose attitude
Recovery
1. Move the control column centrally forward to reduce AoA
2. Level the wings with aileron only after AoA is reduced
3. Apply full power if available and counter any pitch-up
4. Accelerate and retract flap and gear as needed
5. Balance with rudder
Always follow the AFM stall and spin technique. Height loss is small if you act at the first stall warning
Staying out of trouble
Select the right power and attitude for each phase and trim to hold them
Check attitude and airspeed regularly and re-check after any distraction
Practise at safe altitudes and ask an instructor if unsure
Read the AFM or POH for your aircraft

sum.What a stall is: It depends on angle of attack, not speed.
sum.Load factor and stall speed: Stall speed goes up with the square root of g.
sum.Common causes: Distraction, engine failure, go-around and VFR into IMC.
sum.Symptoms: Buffet, nose attitude and falling speed warn you.
sum.Recovery: Forward stick, wings level, power, accelerate, rudder.

cards.q: What controls whether a wing stalls?
Can a stall happen at high airspeed?
cards.a: Yes, at any airspeed or attitude if the critical AoA is exceeded.

cards.q: Stall speed in a 60° banked level turn?
Load factor in a 60° banked level turn?

cards.a: Move the control column forward to reduce AoA.

cards.q: Why not use aileron first in a stall?
cards.a: Aileron on a stalled wing can aggravate roll. Reduce AoA first.

cards.q: What follows significant yaw in a stall?
Why is turning back after engine failure on take-off dangerous?
cards.a: Speed decays and AoA rises, so a stall or spin is likely.

cards.q: Does full power on a go-around guarantee safety?
cards.a: No. Airspeed can still fall so lower the nose to accelerate.

cards.q: Stall speed changes with what mathematical relationship?
cards.a: The square root of load factor.

quiz.q: A level turn at 60° bank has a stall speed of 50 kt in straight flight. The turning stall speed is about:
quiz.why: 2 g multiplies stall speed by about 1.4, so roughly 70 kt.

quiz.q: The first action to recover from a stall is to:
o: Move the control column forward to reduce AoA
quiz.why: Reduce AoA first, then level wings, add power and accelerate.
A stall depends on AoA, which can be exceeded at any speed or attitude.

quiz.q: After engine failure on take-off the leaflet advises you to:
quiz.why: Lower the nose to keep flying speed. Turning back and stretching the glide often cause stalls.

quiz.q: Which is a developed stall symptom?
o: Strong buffet with a high descent rate despite a high nose attitude
quiz.why: A developed stall gives strong buffet, mushy controls and a high descent rate.

quiz.q: Why is a spin more serious than a stall?
o: It needs far more height to recover
It is only a risk with flaps
quiz.why: A spin needs considerably more height to recover from, and may be unrecoverable at low level.
